435.title: Sohila close
435.hook: five hymns to sleep on: praise, one sun, the sky's aarti, the city, now
435.howItsDone: Sikhs read or listen to Kirtan Sohila every night before sleep, and in gurdwaras it is recited as the Guru Granth Sahib is closed and carried to rest in the sukhasan ceremony.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the wedding song at a funeral, and your line: going home. Did you let the day go last night with praise and trust? Today we close Kirtan Sohila. Day four hundred thirty-five.

Every night in a gurdwara there's a quiet moment most visitors never see. The evening singing ends. The Guru Granth Sahib, open since dawn, is closed, wrapped in cloth, and carried with care to its resting room, often lifted on someone's head while the sangat stands. The ceremony is called sukhasan, the position of rest. And as the scripture goes to rest, the words in the air are Sohila. Two weeks ago we opened these five hymns. Tonight, the whole of it.
screen: `THE SCRIPTURE IS CLOSED.` → `SUKHASAN: THE POSITION OF REST.` → `THE WORDS IN THE AIR: SOHILA.`

segments.voice: Here are the five hymns, the way you might remember them lying in the dark. One, Guru Nanak: the house of praise. Jai ghar keerat: in the house where the Creator's praise is spoken and reflected on, sing. And the wedding at its end: the date is written, friends pour oil at the door, the bride is called. Two, Guru Nanak: six schools, six teachers, six teachings, one Guru of gurus in many forms. And its picture: many seasons, one sun. Three, Guru Nanak: the sky's aarti. Gagan mai thaal: the sky is the platter, sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls, the wind the fan, the forests the flowers. The whole world offering. Four, Guru Ram Das: the city. Kaam karodh: desire and anger crowd the body's streets, the thorn of ego pricks with every step, and meeting the holy breaks them up. Five, Guru Arjan: now. Karau benantee: listen, friends, life runs down day and night; this is the time to serve, and make me the dust of the holy's feet. Look at the movement. A doorway, then the calendar, then the sky, then back inside the body, then a friend leaning close. Praise, unity, wonder, honesty, urgency. And then sleep. That's the shape Sikhs lie down inside every night, and the same shape sung when a life is done. A whole evening, and a whole life, held between praise at the beginning and humility at the end.
screen: `ONE: THE HOUSE OF PRAISE.` · `TWO AND THREE: ONE SUN, THE SKY'S AARTI.` · `FOUR: THE CITY OF THIEVES.` · `FIVE: NOW IS THE TIME.` · then, large: `SLEEP IN PRAISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read Sohila tonight. Find it in a gutka, an app, or a recording, and read or listen to all five hymns before bed, even if you only follow the sound. Right now, sit for a moment and walk through the five in your mind: the house, the sun, the sky, the city, the friend. Give each one a breath. On the last breath, picture the day being wrapped up and laid to rest, like the scripture at sukhasan. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Sohila close. Five hymns by three Gurus, said at bedtime and at the end of a life: praise, one sun, the sky's aarti, the city, and now.
Your line: sleep in praise. Tonight, make the last words you hear or say something good: a hymn, a thank-you, the name of someone you love. Day four hundred thirty-five.

436.title: The jewel of peace
436.hook: Sukhmani means the jewel of peace; many read it daily or in groups when life is hard
436.howItsDone: Many Sikhs read Sukhmani Sahib daily, often in the morning, and families and sangats gather to read it together in times of illness, grief, celebration and new beginnings, such as moving into a new home.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed Kirtan Sohila, and your line was sleep in praise. Were the last words you heard last night good ones? Today a new bani begins, the longest of this year. Day four hundred thirty-six.

Walk into a Sikh home the week someone's in the hospital. Or the week a family moves into a new house. Or the night before an exam, or the month after a funeral. There's a good chance you'll find a few people sitting together on the floor or on sofas, each holding a small book, reading aloud in a low, steady rhythm. Sometimes it's a group of women from the neighborhood who gather every week to do exactly this. What they're reading, very often, is Sukhmani Sahib. When life is hard, this is the bani many Sikhs reach for.
screen: `A HOSPITAL WEEK, A NEW HOUSE.` → `PEOPLE READING ALOUD TOGETHER.` → `THE BANI THEY REACH FOR: SUKHMANI.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani. Sukh means peace, comfort, ease, the opposite of dukh, pain. Mani means a jewel; some also hear man, the mind, in it. So Sukhmani is the jewel of peace, or the peace of the mind. Sahib is added out of respect. It was composed by Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, the same Guru who wrote Sohila's last hymn and compiled the scripture. Tradition says he wrote it at a quiet pool near Amritsar called Ramsar, around the time the scripture was being gathered. It sits in Raag Gauri, beginning on Ang 262 of the Guru Granth Sahib. And it's long. Twenty-four sections, each one opening with a short salok and followed by eight stanzas. Near the beginning, Guru Arjan gives the whole bani its own name in a line Sikhs return to again and again. In paraphrase: Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, is the nectar of God's Name; it rests in the minds of the devoted. Notice what that line says peace is. Not a feeling you chase. Not a place you get to after the problems are solved. Peace is the Name, remembering God, and it rests in a mind the way a jewel rests in a box. That's why people reach for it when life is hard. The hospital room doesn't change. The test is still tomorrow. But the Sikh hope is that something steady can rest in the middle of it. Over the next hundred days, we'll walk through Sukhmani section by section.
screen: `SUKH: PEACE. MANI: A JEWEL.` · `GURU ARJAN, AT RAMSAR.` · `TWENTY-FOUR SECTIONS, EIGHT STANZAS EACH.` · `PEACE RESTS IN A MIND.` · then, large: `THE JEWEL OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to the opening. If you can, find a recording of Sukhmani Sahib and play the first minute or two, just the sound, even if you don't follow the words. If you can't right now, sit quietly and picture one of those living rooms: people side by side, books open, voices low. Let the steadiness of it reach you. Then breathe slowly and notice one place in your body that's tight, and let it soften. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
Sukhmani. The jewel of peace: Guru Arjan's long bani of twenty-four sections, read daily by many Sikhs and in groups when life is hard.
Your line: the jewel of peace. Today, when something hard comes up, imagine a small jewel resting in the middle of it, and come back to that picture once. Day four hundred thirty-six.

437.title: How people read it
437.hook: it takes around ninety minutes; many read one ashtpadi a day
437.tomorrow: Ashtpadi 1, salok: I bow to the Guru
437.howItsDone: Many Sikhs read the whole of Sukhmani Sahib daily or weekly; others read one ashtpadi a day, and families and groups often divide the twenty-four ashtpadis among themselves to complete it together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhmani, and your line: the jewel of peace. Did you picture the jewel in the middle of something hard? Today, how people actually read a bani this long. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

Here's an honest question. If Sukhmani takes well over an hour to read, how does anyone with a job, children and a commute read it at all? A grandmother who reads it every morning at five might finish in about ninety minutes, though some are faster and some slower. A nurse on night shifts might not have ninety minutes in a whole week. And yet both of them can call Sukhmani their bani. The answer isn't a trick. It's in how the text was built, eight stanzas at a time.
screen: `WELL OVER AN HOUR TO READ.` → `A GRANDMOTHER AND A NURSE.` → `THE ANSWER IS IN THE STRUCTURE.`

segments.voice: Sukhmani is made of twenty-four ashtpadis. Asht means eight, a number word that goes back to Sanskrit. Padi comes from pad, a stanza or verse. So an ashtpadi is an eight-stanza section. Each one opens with a short salok, two lines that set the theme, and then the eight stanzas unfold it. Each stanza runs about ten lines. Twenty-four times eight is one hundred ninety-two stanzas in all. That structure is a gift to a busy person. An ashtpadi is a complete thought. It has a beginning, a middle and an end. You can read one in a few minutes and close the book having heard something whole. So people read Sukhmani in many ways. Some read all of it every day, often early in the morning. Some read it through once a week. Many families and groups split it up, a few ashtpadis each, so that together they complete it. And many read just one ashtpadi a day, so that the whole bani comes round in about three and a half weeks. Sikh tradition doesn't set one required pace for Sukhmani. What matters, in the bani's own words, is that the Name rests in the mind. A rushed reading of all twenty-four is not the goal. An attentive reading of one is a real reading. That's the pace we'll take on this path: one ashtpadi at a time, its salok first, then a few days with its stanzas, then a day for living it.
screen: `ASHT: EIGHT. PAD: A STANZA.` · `A SALOK, THEN EIGHT STANZAS.` · `ALL AT ONCE, OR ONE A DAY.` · `ATTENTION OVER SPEED.` · then, large: `ONE ASHTPADI AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan an ashtpadi a week. Think about your actual week, not an ideal one. Where is there a quiet ten minutes? Sunday morning before anyone's up. A lunch break in the car. The bus home on Wednesday. Pick one slot and picture yourself there, a book or a phone in your hand, reading eight stanzas slowly. Then let the plan go and just breathe for a little while, as if that slot had already arrived. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once. The bell holds the time.
How people read it. Sukhmani's twenty-four ashtpadis, each a salok and eight stanzas, read all at once, shared among a group, or one at a time.
Your line: one ashtpadi at a time. Today, put the slot you chose into your calendar, with a reminder, so the plan has somewhere to live. Day four hundred thirty-seven.

438.title: Ashtpadi 1, salok: I bow to the Guru
438.hook: aad gure namah: I bow to the primal Guru, the Guru of the ages, the True Guru (Sukhmani 1)
438.howItsDone: Sikhs who read Sukhmani Sahib begin with this salok of four bows, and many bow before the Guru Granth Sahib whenever they enter its presence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how people read Sukhmani, and your line: one ashtpadi at a time. Did your slot make it into the calendar? Today we open the first one, starting with its salok. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

Before a match, a wrestler in a Punjabi village touches the earth of the pit and then his forehead. A musician touches the strings of an instrument before playing, a dancer bows to the floor. Before Sikhs read from the Guru Granth Sahib, they bow to it. People across many cultures begin serious things the same way: by lowering themselves a little, first. The long road of Sukhmani begins like that too. Before a single teaching, before peace or Name or anything else, Guru Arjan bows. Four times.
screen: `A WRESTLER TOUCHES THE EARTH.` → `SERIOUS THINGS BEGIN WITH A BOW.` → `SUKHMANI OPENS: FOUR BOWS.`

segments.voice: Here is the salok that opens Sukhmani. Aad gure namah. Jugaad gure namah. Satgure namah. Sri gurdeve namah. Each line ends with namah, an old Sanskrit word of homage: I bow, I salute. You may hear it in namaste. So the salok is four bows, each to a slightly different face of the same Guru. Aad gure: the Guru of the beginning, the primal Guru, there before anything began. Jugaad gure: the Guru through all the ages, jug being the great ages of time. Satgure: the True Guru. And Sri gurdeve: the great, divine Guru, the Guru who shines. Who is this Guru? In Gurbani, the Guru is first of all God, the One who teaches. Sikhs also honor the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru's voice in the world, but here the bows go to the One beyond time: the beginning, every age, truth itself. Listen to how the salok moves. It starts at the very beginning, then stretches across all ages, then names what is true, then what shines. A bow that travels from the first moment to this one. Some listeners hear an echo of Japji's opening salok, which praises the One who was true in the beginning and true through the ages. Guru Arjan is setting Sukhmani in the same frame. And notice the order he chooses: the jewel of peace doesn't begin with peace. It begins with bowing. Peace, the bani suggests, starts with the head a little lower than before.
screen: `NAMAH: I BOW.` · `THE PRIMAL GURU, THE GURU OF AGES.` · `THE TRUE GURU, THE DIVINE GURU.` · `PEACE BEGINS WITH A BOW.` · then, large: `I BOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bow your head once. Sit up comfortably. Breathe in. As you breathe out, let your head lower slowly, chin toward your chest, as far as feels easy. Stay there for a breath or two, and notice what it feels like to be lower than a moment ago. Then rise slowly. If you'd like, repeat it, and with each of the four lines in your mind: the beginning, the ages, the true, the divine. If you pray, you can whisper aad gure namah. The bell holds the time.
Ashtpadi 1. The first section of Sukhmani, opened by a salok of four bows: to the primal Guru, the Guru of the ages, the True Guru, the divine Guru.
Your line: I bow. Today, before one serious thing, a meeting, a meal, a hard conversation, lower your head a little for one breath first. Day four hundred thirty-eight.

439.title: Remember, and find peace
439.hook: simro simar simar sukh paavo: remember, remember, and find peace (Sukhmani 1)
439.howItsDone: Sikhs practice simran by repeating the Name, Waheguru, quietly or aloud, alone or together in the sangat; some use a mala of beads to count, and many keep the Name going through the day's ordinary tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhmani's opening salok, and your line: I bow. Did you lower your head before something serious? Today, the first stanza, and the word the whole bani rests on. Day four hundred thirty-nine.
screen: `I BOW — FOUR BOWS TO THE GURU.`

segments.voice: How do you remember a phone number someone just told you? You say it again. And again. Under your breath, all the way to the pen. How do you remember a person who has died? You say their name, tell their stories, keep their photo where you'll see it. Remembering, it turns out, is mostly repetition. Not a single grand act, but something done again and again until it becomes part of you. That is exactly how the first stanza of Sukhmani begins: with one word, said three times in a row.
screen: `A PHONE NUMBER, SAID AGAIN.` → `A NAME, A STORY, A PHOTO.` → `REMEMBERING IS REPETITION.`

segments.voice: The first stanza opens: simro simar simar sukh paavo. I remember, and remembering, remembering, I find peace. Then, in paraphrase: and the troubles and anguish of the body are erased. The word under all of it is simran. It comes from the Sanskrit smarana, remembering, from a root meaning to remember or call to mind. In Sikh life, simran means remembering God, and in practice it often means repeating the Name, Waheguru, quietly or aloud, again and again. Listen to how the line performs what it describes. Simro, simar, simar: the word itself is repeated, three beats before the reward arrives. Sukh paavo: I find peace. Sukh, the same sukh as in Sukhmani. So the jewel of peace you met two days ago is found, right here at the start, by remembering. The stanza goes on to say, in paraphrase, that the Vedas, the Puranas and the Simritis, the great scriptures of Guru Arjan's world, were made from the one word of the Name. And that the person in whose heart even a tiny particle of it lives has a glory no one can count. Then it closes, as the stanzas will, with Nanak's voice: those who long only for the sight of You, save me with them. Here's what makes simran different from just thinking about God. Thinking is something you do once and finish. Simran is a practice. It's a phone number said over and over until your mouth knows it before your mind does. The stanza promises that peace is found in that repeating.
screen: `SIMRO SIMAR SIMAR: REMEMBER, AGAIN.` · `SIMRAN, FROM SMARANA.` · `THE ONE WORD THE SCRIPTURES CAME FROM.` · `A PRACTICE, NOT A THOUGHT.` · then, large: `REMEMBER, FIND PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repeat the Name ten times. If you pray, say Waheguru, slowly, ten times, aloud or in your head, letting each one ride on an out-breath. If that isn't your practice, choose a word that steadies you, peace, or thank you, or a name you love, and repeat it the same way. Count on your fingers if it helps. Don't hurry toward ten. When you reach it, sit in the quiet afterward and notice what's different, if anything. The bell holds the time.
Simran. Remembering God, often by repeating the Name; Sukhmani's first stanza says that remembering, again and again, brings peace.

Your line: remember, find peace. Today, pick one repeated moment, every time you unlock your phone, every time you wash your hands, and let it carry one quiet Waheguru, or your own steady word. Day four hundred thirty-nine.

440.title: What remembering does
440.hook: in remembering God there is no pain, and death does not frighten (Sukhmani 1)
440.howItsDone: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite these stanzas of the first ashtpadi with their repeated opening, prabh kai simran, and many turn to them especially in times of illness or fear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, simran, and your line: remember, find peace. Did one repeated moment carry a quiet word for you? Today, the stanzas that say what remembering does. Day four hundred forty.

An umbrella doesn't stop the rain. It doesn't shorten the storm or change the forecast. It changes one thing: what the rain does to you. You still walk the same street, in the same weather, and arrive less soaked. Much of what people carry through a hard day works like that: a hand to hold, a song, a photo in a wallet. The first ashtpadi of Sukhmani lists, line after line, what remembering God does for the one who remembers. Read closely, it sounds less like a forecast and more like an umbrella. Today: what remembering does.
screen: `AN UMBRELLA DOESN'T STOP THE RAIN.` → `IT CHANGES WHAT THE RAIN DOES TO YOU.` → `WHAT REMEMBERING DOES.`

segments.voice: The phrase is prabh kai simran: in the remembrance of God. And the second stanza of the first ashtpadi hangs line after line on it. In paraphrase: in the remembrance of God, one does not enter the womb again. In the remembrance of God, the pain of death flees. In the remembrance of God, death is set aside. In the remembrance of God, enemies turn back. In the remembrance of God, no obstacle blocks the way. In the remembrance of God, one stays awake day and night. In the remembrance of God, fear does not touch you. In the remembrance of God, sorrow does not burn. And the stanzas that follow keep the drum going, line after line, through the rest of the ashtpadi: in the remembrance of God come wisdom, meditation and understanding; the remembering one becomes truly wealthy, truly honored. Notice what the list is doing. It isn't promising that nothing bad will happen. Sikhs who read Sukhmani in hospital rooms know that pain and loss still come. It's describing what changes inside the one who remembers. Fear doesn't get the same grip. Death, which frightens everyone, is set aside, not abolished but put in its place. Sikhs believe that remembering God frees the soul from the round of birth and death, which is why the stanza speaks of the womb. And on an ordinary day, it means this: the one who remembers carries something that the frightening thing cannot reach.
screen: `PRABH KAI SIMRAN: IN GOD'S REMEMBRANCE.` · `LINE AFTER LINE ON ONE BEAT.` · `FEAR DOES NOT TOUCH; SORROW DOESN'T BURN.` · `NOT NO PAIN: PAIN IN ITS PLACE.` · then, large: `NO FEAR IN REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember during one hard moment. Bring to mind something today or this week that frightens you a little: a test result, a bill, a conversation, a long night ahead. Don't push it away. Look at it. Now breathe in, and on the out-breath, if you pray, say Waheguru, or simply say to yourself: remembering. Do that four or five times, the hard thing still in view. Notice whether its grip loosens even slightly. Then rest. The bell holds the time.
What remembering does. Sukhmani's repeated phrase, prabh kai simran: in God's remembrance, fear does not touch, sorrow does not burn, and death is set aside.
Your line: no fear in remembering. Today, the next time something makes your stomach drop, try the stanza's phrase before anything else: in the remembrance of God. Day four hundred forty.

441.title: Living ashtpadi 1
441.hook: Guru Arjan begins with the simplest practice: remember
441.howItsDone: Many Sikhs carry the first ashtpadi's teaching into the day by repeating Waheguru during ordinary tasks, and by joining the sangat, where Sukhmani says remembrance of God is found.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line was no fear in remembering. This is a week's end: we closed Sohila, opened Sukhmani, bowed four times, met simran and its drum. Today, living the first ashtpadi. Day four hundred forty-one.
screen: `NO FEAR IN REMEMBERING.` · `A WEEK: SOHILA'S CLOSE, SUKHMANI'S START.`

segments.voice: If you were writing the great bani of peace, where would you start? With a philosophy of suffering? A ladder of spiritual stages, beginner to master? A list of rules? Guru Arjan had compiled the scripture. He knew every hymn of the Gurus before him. He could have begun anywhere. He began with the simplest thing a human being can do, the thing a child can do, the thing you do every time you think of someone you love. He began with remembering.
screen: `WHERE WOULD YOU START?` → `A PHILOSOPHY? A LADDER? RULES?` → `GURU ARJAN STARTS WITH REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: Look back at the whole first ashtpadi. The salok bows four times. The first stanza says: remember, remembering again and again, and find peace. The next ones beat the drum, prabh kai simran: in God's remembrance, fear does not touch, sorrow does not burn. And as the ashtpadi goes on, it widens the circle. In paraphrase: those who remember God are the ones who are truly rich, truly honored, truly at rest. Then, near the end, the ashtpadi says something important about where remembering happens. In paraphrase: the remembrance of God comes in the company of the holy, and it comes to those to whom God gives it. So simran isn't presented as a feat of willpower. It grows in company, the sangat. And Sikhs understand it as a gift as much as an effort, which is why Sikh prayer so often asks for it rather than claiming it. That's a gentle thing to begin with. The first ashtpadi doesn't ask you to be holy. It asks you to remember, among good people, and to ask for the remembering when it won't come. Here's what living it might look like on an ordinary Tuesday. A reminder on your phone that says only: remember. The name Waheguru, or your own steady word, on the walk from the car. A friend you sit with who makes remembering easier. Not grand. Just repeated. Guru Arjan starts there because everything else in Sukhmani is built on it.
screen: `THE BOW, THE WORD, THE DRUM.` · `THE ONES WHO REMEMBER ARE RICH.` · `REMEMBERING GROWS IN COMPANY.` · `A GIFT AS MUCH AS AN EFFORT.` · then, large: `BEGIN WITH REMEMBERING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set one reminder today. Take out your phone, if it's nearby, and set one reminder for later today, at a time you'll actually see it. Make the label one word: remember. Or Waheguru, if you pray. Then put the phone down, face down, and sit. Practice the remembering now, so the reminder later has somewhere to land: a few slow breaths, the Name or your word on each one. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 1. Sukhmani's first section in daily life: bow, remember again and again, and let the remembering grow in good company.
Your line: begin with remembering. When the reminder goes off today, stop whatever you're doing for one breath, and remember. Day four hundred forty-one.
